title: Sequences
competency: Find terms of a sequence from its general term or a recursion formula.

keywords.def: A list of numbers in a definite order made by a rule.
The rule aₙ that gives the nth term.
A sequence with a last term.
A sequence with no last term.
A sequence where each term is made from the terms before it.
The rule that makes the next term from earlier terms.

en.text: A sequence is a list of numbers in a definite order made by a rule. The general term aₙ is the rule: put n = 1, 2, 3, and so on to get the terms. A finite sequence has a last term; an infinite one does not. Its graph is separate dots, never a joined line.

am.text: ቅደም ተከተል (ሲኩዌንስ) በአንድ ሕግ መሠረት በቅደም ተከተል የተደረደሩ ቁጥሮች ዝርዝር ነው። አጠቃላይ ተርም aₙ ሕጉ ነው፤ n = 1, 2, 3 በማስገባት ተርሞቹን እናገኛለን።

screens.title: Planting trees in rows
screens.text: A community plants 20 trees in the 1st row, 34 in the 2nd row and 48 in the 3rd row, and so on.
screens.ask: How many trees are in the 5th row?
screens.after:
Find the jump: 34 − 20 = 14 and 48 − 34 = 14.
Keep adding 14: 48 + 14 = 62 (4th row), 62 + 14 = 76 (5th row).
So the 5th row has 76 trees. (62 is the 4th row, a common slip.)
A list made by a rule like this is a sequence.

screens.title: Sequences
paras: A sequence is an arrangement of numbers in a definite order by some rule.
Sequences help us predict, evaluate and monitor what happens next.
A sequence is a function. Its domain is the integers n ≥ m, usually from 0 or 1.
The values a₁, a₂, a₃, … are the terms. aₙ is the general term (the nth term).

screens.title: Two types of sequence
paras: The type depends on whether there is a last term.

screens.title: Finite or infinite?
screens.ask: Tap each sequence. Does it have a last term?
items: Finite: the last term is 10. Domain 1, 2, …, 10.
Infinite: the dots “…” mean it never stops. Domain ℕ.
Infinite: there is a term for every n.

screens.title: Make terms from a rule
screens.ask: Move n. Watch the term aₙ = 2n − 1 change.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A list of numbers in a definite order made by a rule.
The rule aₙ that gives the nth term.
A sequence with a last term.
A sequence with no last term.

screens.text: Find a term from the general term: for aₙ = 2n − 1, what is a₄?
screens.why:
Step 1: a₄ means put n = 4.
Step 2: a₄ = 2(4) − 1.
Step 3: 2 × 4 = 8, and 8 − 1 = 7.
So a₄ = 7. (9 is a₅; 8 forgets the − 1.)

screens.title: aₙ = (−1/3)ⁿ⁻¹: first five terms
steps: a₁ = (−1/3)⁰ = 1. Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1.
a₃ = (−1/3)² = (−1)²/3² = 1/9. An even power of a negative is positive.
a₄ = (−1/3)³ = (−1)³/3³ = −1/27. An odd power is negative.

screens.title: The graph of a sequence
paras: Plot each pair (n, aₙ) as a separate dot.
Do not join the dots: n takes only whole-number values.

screens.title: Figure 1.1: the dots of aₙ = 2n + 1
screens.ask: Tap each dot. Read n across and aₙ up.

points.name: a₅
points.info: n = 5: 2(5) + 1 = 11. The dots are not joined.

screens.ask: Find the 3rd term of aₙ = n/(n + 1): a₃ = ___
screens.why:
Step 1: put n = 3 in the top and the bottom.
Step 2: a₃ = 3/(3 + 1).
Step 3: 3 + 1 = 4, so a₃ = 3/4.
Check: 3/4 = 0.75.
screens.clue: Put n = 3 on top and in the bottom.

screens.ask: Find the 5th term of aₙ = n³: a₅ = ___
screens.why:
Step 1: put n = 5: a₅ = 5³.
Step 2: 5³ = 5 × 5 × 5.
Step 3: 5 × 5 = 25, and 25 × 5 = 125.
So a₅ = 125. (Trap: 5³ is not 5 × 3 = 15.)

screens.text: List the first four terms of the alternating sequence aₙ = (−1)ⁿ.
screens.why:
Step 1: n = 1: (−1)¹ = −1.
Step 2: n = 2: (−1)² = (−1)(−1) = 1.
Step 3: n = 3 gives −1 again; n = 4 gives 1.
Odd power → −1, even power → 1.
So the terms are −1, 1, −1, 1. (1, −1, 1, −1 would start at n = 0.)

screens.text: Graph of a sequence: true or false? The dots of a sequence graph should be joined with a line.
screens.why:
A sequence is only defined at n = 1, 2, 3, …
There is no term a₁.₅ between a₁ and a₂.
So the graph is separate dots, not a line.
The statement is false.

screens.ask: Find a later term from a pattern: Bontu has 130 birr in month 1, 210 birr in month 2 and 290 birr in month 3. In month 7 she has ___ birr.
screens.why:
Step 1: find the monthly increase: 210 − 130 = 80, 290 − 210 = 80.
Step 2: month 7 is 6 months after month 1.
Step 3: a₇ = 130 + 6 × 80 = 130 + 480 = 610.
Check by listing: 290, 370, 450, 530, 610.
So she has 610 birr. (Trap: 130 + 7 × 80 = 690 counts one jump too many.)
screens.clue: Find how much is added each month.

screens.text: Find the general term: which rule gives the sequence 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, …?
screens.why:
Step 1: the gaps are 3, 5, 7, 9. They grow, so the rule is not linear like 3n − 1.
Step 2: compare with the squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.
Step 3: each term is one more than a square: aₙ = n² + 1.
Check n = 4: 16 + 1 = 17 ✓.
(3n − 1 gives 2, 5, 8: it fails at n = 3.)
screens.clue: The gaps between terms are not equal. Try squares.

en.text: A recursive sequence gives the first terms and a rule that makes each new term from the terms before it. Fibonacci starts 1, 1 and adds the two previous terms. The Ethiopian mathematician Mulatu Lemma's sequence starts 4, 1 with the same adding rule.

am.text: ሪከርሲቭ ቅደም ተከተል የመጀመሪያዎቹን ተርሞች ይሰጣል፤ እያንዳንዱ አዲስ ተርም ከቀደሙት ተርሞች ይሠራል። ፊቦናቺ 1, 1 ብሎ ይጀምራል፤ የሙላቱ ለማ ቅደም ተከተል 4, 1 ብሎ ይጀምራል።

screens.title: Squares that make a rectangle
screens.ask: Squares of side 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 fill a rectangle 8 by 13. What side comes next?
screens.after:
Look at the sides: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.
Each side is the sum of the two before it: 1 + 1 = 2, 1 + 2 = 3, 2 + 3 = 5, 3 + 5 = 8.
So the next side is 5 + 8 = 13.
This is the Fibonacci pattern.

screens.title: Fibonacci's sequence
paras: Leonardo Fibonacci (about 1170–1240) was an Italian mathematician.
He studied how rabbit pairs breed month by month: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, …
Each number is the sum of the two numbers before it.

people.name: Leonardo Fibonacci
people.did: Made advances in number theory and algebra. Known for the Fibonacci sequence.

people.name: Mulatu Lemma
people.did: Ethiopian mathematician (Addis Ababa University, Kent State University). Introduced the Mulatu numbers in 2011.

screens.title: Mulatu sequence
paras: Professor Mulatu Lemma is an Ethiopian mathematician.
His sequence uses the Fibonacci adding rule with different first terms.

screens.title: Fibonacci and Mulatu side by side
screens.ask: Move n. Both use “add the two before”. Only the start differs.
screens.note: Same rule, different first terms, different sequence.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A sequence where each term is made from the terms before it.
The rule that makes the next term from earlier terms.

screens.text: Use the Fibonacci rule (add the two terms before): 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … What comes after 13?
screens.why:
Step 1: the rule is Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂.
Step 2: the two terms before the new one are 8 and 13.
Step 3: 8 + 13 = 21.
So the next term is 21. (26 doubles 13; that is not the rule.)
screens.clue: Add the two terms before it.

screens.ask: Use the Fibonacci rule to find the 12th term of 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …: ___
screens.why:
Step 1: 8 is the 6th term. Keep adding the last two.
Step 2: 5 + 8 = 13 (7th), 8 + 13 = 21 (8th), 13 + 21 = 34 (9th).
Step 3: 21 + 34 = 55 (10th), 34 + 55 = 89 (11th), 55 + 89 = 144 (12th).
So the 12th term is 144.
screens.clue: Keep adding the last two terms until you have 12 terms.

screens.ask: Use the Mulatu rule Mₙ = Mₙ₋₁ + Mₙ₋₂ (M₀ = 4, M₁ = 1). Find M₈ = ___
screens.why:
Step 1: list the terms: 4, 1, 5, 6, 11, 17, 28, 45 (M₀ to M₇).
Step 2: M₈ = M₇ + M₆.
Step 3: 45 + 28 = 73.
So M₈ = 73.

screens.ask: Squares in the Fibonacci rectangle: add the areas 1² + 1² + 2² + 3² + 5² + 8² = ___
screens.why:
Step 1: square each side: 1, 1, 4, 9, 25, 64.
Step 2: add: 1 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 15; 15 + 25 = 40; 40 + 64 = 104.
Check: the squares fill an 8 × 13 rectangle, and 8 × 13 = 104 ✓.
So the sum is 104.

screens.text: Recursion formulas: true or false? A recursive rule needs the first term or terms to be given.
screens.why:
A recursion makes each term from the terms before it.
To find M₂ = M₁ + M₀ you must already know M₀ and M₁.
Without a start there is nothing to add.
So the statement is true.
screens.clue: What is M₂ if you do not know M₀?

screens.ask: Use the recursion a₀ = 2, a₁ = 3, aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂. The first term bigger than 50 is ___
screens.why:
Step 1: 2 + 3 = 5, 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 8 = 13.
Step 2: 8 + 13 = 21, 13 + 21 = 34.
Step 3: 21 + 34 = 55.
Check: 34 < 50 but 55 > 50.
So the first term bigger than 50 is 55.
screens.clue: List terms by adding the last two until you pass 50.

items.ask: List the terms of aₙ = 2n: a₁, …, a₅ = 2, 4, 6, 8, ___
items.why:
Step 1: the 5th term is a₅.
Step 2: put n = 5: a₅ = 2(5).
Step 3: 2 × 5 = 10.
So the list is 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.

items.ask: Find the 5th term of aₙ = (1/2)ⁿ⁻¹: a₅ = ___
items.why:
Step 1: put n = 5: the power is n − 1 = 4.
Step 2: a₅ = (1/2)⁴ = 1⁴/2⁴.
Step 3: 2⁴ = 16, so a₅ = 1/16.
Check: 1/16 = 0.0625. (Trap: using power 5 gives 1/32.)

items.ask: Find the 5th term of aₙ = n/(n + 1): a₅ = ___
items.why:
Step 1: put n = 5 in the top and the bottom.
Step 2: a₅ = 5/(5 + 1).
Step 3: 5 + 1 = 6, so a₅ = 5/6.

Step 1: the dot for n = 5 is (5, a₅).
Step 2: a₅ = 3(5) − 1 = 15 − 1 = 14.
Check: the dots rise by 3 each step: 11 + 3 = 14.
So the dot is (5, 14).

items.text: Graph of aₙ = 1/n: what happens to the dots as n grows?
opts: They fall towards 0 but stay positive
They lie on a straight line
items.ans: They fall towards 0 but stay positive
items.why:
Step 1: a₁ = 1, a₂ = 1/2, a₃ = 1/3, a₄ = 1/4, a₅ = 1/5.
Step 2: the bottom grows, so each term is smaller.
Step 3: 1/n is always positive and never 0.
So the dots fall towards 0 but stay positive.
(They are not on a line: the drops 1/2, 1/6, 1/12 are not equal.)

items.ask: Find the next term: Bontu has 130, 210 and 290 birr in the first three months. In month 4 she has ___ birr.
items.why:
Step 1: the increase is 210 − 130 = 80 each month.
Step 2: check: 290 − 210 = 80 ✓.
Step 3: month 4: 290 + 80 = 370.
So she has 370 birr.
items.clue: She adds the same amount every month.

items.ask: Fibonacci rule: the 12th term of 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, … is ___
items.why:
Step 1: 8 is the 6th term.
Step 2: add the last two each time: 13, 21, 34 (7th to 9th).
Step 3: 55, 89, 144 (10th to 12th).
So the 12th term is 144.
items.clue: Add the two terms before it.

items.text: Use the Mulatu rule (M₀ = 4, M₁ = 1, add the two before). Which list gives the first eight terms?
items.why:
Step 1: start with M₀ = 4 and M₁ = 1.
Step 2: M₂ = 1 + 4 = 5, M₃ = 5 + 1 = 6, M₄ = 6 + 5 = 11.
Step 3: M₅ = 17, M₆ = 28, M₇ = 45.
So: 4, 1, 5, 6, 11, 17, 28, 45.
(4, 1, 3, 4, … subtracts; 1, 1, 2, … is Fibonacci.)

test.text: Find a term from the general term: for aₙ = 3n + 2, what is a₆?

test.ask: Find the 4th term of aₙ = (−2)ⁿ⁻¹: a₄ = ___
test.why:
Put n = 4: the power is 4 − 1 = 3.
(−2)³ = (−2)(−2)(−2).
(−2)(−2) = 4, and 4 × (−2) = −8.
An odd power of a negative is negative: a₄ = −8.

test.text: Types of sequence: true or false? An infinite sequence has a last term.
test.why:
An infinite sequence goes on for all natural numbers n.
It has no last term.
Only a finite sequence has a last term.
So the statement is false.

test.ask: Use the recursion a₀ = 1, a₁ = 4, aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂. Find a₄ = ___
test.why:
a₂ = a₁ + a₀ = 4 + 1 = 5.
a₃ = a₂ + a₁ = 5 + 4 = 9.
a₄ = a₃ + a₂ = 9 + 5 = 14.
So a₄ = 14.

test.text: Find the general term: which rule gives 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, …?
test.why:
The top is the term number n: 1, 2, 3, 4.
The bottom is one more: n + 1.
So aₙ = n/(n + 1).
Check n = 3: 3/4 ✓. ((n + 1)/n gives 2, 3/2: upside down.)

notes.text: Fibonacci example (p.7): the book asks for the first eight terms but its table and graph show ten (F₀ to F₉). Values are correct.
Book counts Fibonacci from F₀, so the 12th term listed (144) is F₁₁. Lessons use "12th term" as the book's Exercise 1.2 does.
